ego.name: Grace Hopper
ego.summary: Grace Hopper was an American computer scientist, mathematician, and United States Navy rear admiral. She programmed the Harvard Mark I, developed compiler systems including FLOW-MATIC, and helped create COBOL.

connections.relationship_description: Hopper's father and a member of the New York family in which she grew up.
connections.notes: He and Mary Campbell Van Horne raised Hopper in a family that attended West End Collegiate Church.

connections.relationship_description: Hopper's mother, who discovered seven-year-old Grace dismantling alarm clocks to learn how they worked.
connections.notes: At age seven, Hopper dismantled seven alarm clocks before her mother stopped her.

connections.relationship_description: New York University professor whom Grace Murray married in 1930.
connections.notes: She retained the surname Hopper after their divorce and did not remarry.

connections.relationship_description: Yale mathematician who directed Hopper's 1934 doctoral dissertation, New Types of Irreducibility Criteria.
connections.notes: Hopper's doctorate was in mathematics and mathematical physics.

connections.relationship_description: Leader of the Harvard Mark I team that Hopper joined in 1944. They later co-authored three papers on the Mark I.
connections.notes: Hopper remained at Harvard's Computation Laboratory under a Navy contract until 1949.

connections.relationship_description: Co-founder of the Eckert–Mauchly Computer Corporation, which brought Hopper into the UNIVAC I project in 1949.
connections.notes: The company was later acquired by Remington Rand, where Hopper continued her compiler work.

connections.relationship_description: Co-founder of the Eckert–Mauchly Computer Corporation, where Hopper joined the UNIVAC I team in 1949.
connections.notes: Mauchly co-founded the firm with J. Presper Eckert.

connections.relationship_description: COBOL developer who served with Hopper on the 1959 CODASYL effort.
connections.notes: COBOL extended Hopper's FLOW-MATIC language and incorporated ideas from other business-language work.

connections.relationship_description: Computer scientist who worked with Hopper on early standards for the COBOL and FORTRAN programming languages.
connections.notes: Their work connected early programming practice with later language-standardization efforts.

connections.relationship_description: Admiral who promoted Hopper to captain in the United States Navy in 1973.
connections.notes: The promotion occurred during Hopper's leadership of the Navy Programming Languages Group.

connections.notes: Hopper held the DEC position until her death in 1992.

category_summaries.summary: Hopper grew up in New York with Walter Fletcher Murray and Mary Campbell Van Horne. Her 1930 marriage to Vincent Foster Hopper gave her the surname she retained after their 1945 divorce.
Hopper studied mathematics at Vassar and Yale before teaching at Vassar. Under Øystein Ore at Yale, she earned a doctorate in mathematics in 1934. She left Vassar on wartime leave in 1943.

Hopper's technical circle spans the Harvard Mark I, UNIVAC I, and the development of business programming languages. Howard Aiken led the Harvard team she joined in 1944. Eckert and Mauchly's company gave her a role on UNIVAC I in 1949. In 1959, she worked with COBOL developers including Jean E. Sammet through CODASYL.

Hopper's Navy career included leadership of the Navy Programming Languages Group and promotion to captain by Elmo R. Zumwalt Jr. After retiring in 1986, she worked as a consulting engineer for Digital Equipment Corporation until her death.
